overview: The Ioway people have a history of river villages, farming, trade and repeated displacement across the central United States. This account includes the distinct Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska and Iowa Tribe of Oklahoma. The imported Oklahoma outline shown in 1492 is anachronistic: a southern migration began in 1878, and that reservation was established in 1883. It must not be read as the location of an Ioway state in 1492.

periods.title: River communities and shifting homelands
periods.summary: An approximate historical window for villages, migration and trade before confinement to a reduced reservation.

periods.title: Reservation and land loss
periods.summary: A reservation along the Great Nemaha River followed treaty cessions; later agreements reduced the land base.

periods.title: A southern community takes shape
periods.summary: Some families left the northern reservation for Indian Territory; others remained.

periods.title: Two continuing tribal governments
periods.summary: The Oklahoma reservation and the northern community developed distinct governments with a shared people’s history.

items.text: Archaeologists connect ancestral Ioway communities with the broad Oneota tradition, also associated with other related peoples. Characteristic finds include shell-tempered pottery, pipestone, copper and small triangular arrowheads. Oneota is an archaeological category, not the name of a single Ioway empire.

Oneota farming equipment included hoes made from bison shoulder blades. Maize, beans and squash grew alongside a food supply obtained through hunting and gathering. The University of Iowa’s teaching collection makes this resourcefulness tangible: an animal bone could become a tool for tending a vegetable field.

Iowaville stood beside the lower Des Moines River near present-day Selma in the late 1700s and early 1800s. Kettle fragments, hoes, trade beads and metal ornaments survive from village life. Repaired and reshaped objects show residents adapting traded goods to their own needs.

Magnetometers and ground-penetrating radar helped archaeologists look beneath Iowaville’s plowed surface. Testing revealed surviving houses and storage pits. The fields had disturbed the upper soil, but portions of the village remained below: an underground record of where people lived and stored supplies.

William Green’s study of Iowaville emphasizes deer hunting and hide exports. Pipes made from red and gray-green stone connected the village with distant sources and social alliances. French-Indigenous families also helped shape trade networks, so commerce involved relatives and relationships as well as merchandise.

In 1837, Ioway leaders presented a map of ancestral villages and travel routes to United States officials to defend their land claims. Known as the No-Heart Map after one of its presenters, it placed remembered history on paper. Its name does not establish a sole artist.

Iowaville’s departure story remains complicated. A much-repeated account of a single devastating Sauk attack is not established by the evidence summarized by the state archaeologist. Population movement occurred amid disease, conflict, trade changes and pressure on land; the village’s end was not the end of the people.

The 1854 Kansas-Nebraska Act drew a territorial line across the northern reservation. That helps explain the present tribe’s two-state name. The tribal government identifies the treaty of March 6, 1861, as establishing its current reservation boundaries, a later legal geography rather than an ancient frontier.

Dissatisfaction with conditions on the northern reservation led some Ioway families to move to Indian Territory in 1878. An executive order established their Oklahoma reservation on August 15, 1883. Other families remained in the north, and the resulting governments are separate institutions.

The Oklahoma tribe’s oral-history project recorded elders’ memories and gathered family photographs and genealogies. It also describes winter storytelling gatherings. Keeping the sound of an elder’s voice gives later generations something a family tree alone cannot preserve: how a relative actually told a story.

The tribe’s January 2015 newsletter prints Bah Kho-Je Xla Chi and translates the name as “Grey Snow Eagle House.” This is an attested modern Ioway-language institutional name. Its spelling is reproduced from that particular publication, not offered as an ancient inscription or a universal spelling standard.

The Iowa Tribe of Oklahoma opened Grey Snow Eagle House in January 2006. Its work combines rehabilitation, permanent homes for birds that cannot return to the wild, education and research. Caring for eagles became a sustained tribal institution with practical conservation work.

At the eagle house, permanently injured birds receive food, veterinary care, enrichment and rock pools for bathing. Recovering birds practice in a 150-foot flight cage with a turn before release. Staff assess strength and hunting ability: passing flight school requires more than flapping enthusiastically.

In the northern community, the Iowa and Sac & Fox mission building, constructed in 1845-46, returned to tribal custody with ten acres in October 2021. The tribe describes the museum as part of recovering culture and land. A former missionary institution now supports a community-led account of its past.

ending.text: The Ioway continue through families and distinct tribal governments in Kansas and Nebraska and in Oklahoma. Land cessions, relocation and reservation divisions transformed their political geography. The map’s imported cutoff years are not dates of disappearance.
